1:
The title is disputed first, because the Hebrew has none. Clarke reports that neither Hebrew nor Chaldee gives the psalm a heading, and that where the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic and Arabic supply one — a song of David for the day preceding the Sabbath, when the earth was founded — there is no information in it on which any man can rely; twelve manuscripts of Kennicott and De Rossi write it as part of the psalm before, and thinks it was probably written at the close of the captivity by Levites. Augustine takes that same supplied title seriously. The sixth day is meant, on which the animals were made and last of all man in God's likeness; and the order was not arbitrary, since the ages were to run a like course before we rest in God. But we rest only if we do good works — for God rested on the seventh day not from weariness, nor has he left off working, since our Lord says his Father worketh hitherto.

What the acclamation means Ellicott settles by usage. Better, he says, Jehovah has become king: the usual term for ascending a throne, used in Isaiah of the re-establishment of the State after the Captivity, and taken up by the last of Israel's poets in a strain that looks beyond this world. The robing and girding are part of the ceremony of inauguration, and the clauses run better as majesty he has put on, Jehovah has put it on, with strength has he girded himself — Jehovah as a warrior arranging himself for battle. Spurgeon hears a throne briefly seeming vacant: as if the Lord had for a while appeared to leave it, and on a sudden puts on his regal apparel and ascends his lofty seat, while his happy people proclaim him with new joy. Let us repeat the proclamation, whispering it to the desponding and publishing it in the face of the foe.

On the clothing itself the comment turns comparative. Henry calls God's dominion the thing we are most concerned to believe next to his being — King not of right only but in fact, disposing of all creatures according to the counsel of his own will — and measures the majesty by contrast: that of earthly princes beside God's terrible majesty is the glimmering of a glow-worm beside the sun going forth in his strength. And he is clothed not only with majesty, as a prince in his court, but with strength, as a general in the field. Spurgeon adds that he is clothed not with emblems of majesty but with majesty itself, not the semblance but the reality of sovereignty; Wesley says the majesty and strength he always had he will now show in the eyes of all people, overruling the world's confusions so that they end in erecting a kingdom that cannot be moved.

Whose throne it is Gill and Calvin answer differently. Gill reads the whole of the King Messiah, set up from everlasting, reigning through the Old Testament dispensation, come in human nature though his kingdom was not with observation, declared Lord and Christ at his ascension, and one day to reign manifestly — and takes the throne established of old for one prepared from eternity. Calvin keeps the confession where it does its work: our failure to invest God with the power belonging to him, and so despoiling him of his authority, is the source of the fear we so often feel. All admit in word that God reigns, but how few oppose that shield to the hostile powers of the world, that they may fear nothing however terrible? Keil and Delitzsch place the psalm among those that behold the perfected theocracy not as the appearing of a human king but of Jahve himself — a series parallel with the christocratic psalms, converging in the Old Testament but never meeting there.
3:
Whether the floods are water or nations is the question these verses raise, and it is never quite settled. Clarke takes them at once for men: multitudes have confederated against God's people, and troop succeeds troop as the waves succeed each other; the Lord on high is greater in strength than all the nations that can rise against him, so that the most powerful empires prevail nothing, and those who trust him have nothing to fear. Ellicott leaves the matter open, saying it is doubtful whether the description of a raging sea is to be taken literally or as emblematic of war and its horrors. On the words themselves he is exact: the noun rendered waves is better rendered roaring for the sake of the parallelism, though literally it is the breaking of the waves upon the shore; floods here stands poetically for the sea; and the repetition of the verb a third time in a different tense adds to the force, where the Septuagint and Vulgate read instead from the voices of many waters.

Gill answers the same question by naming the enemies. Christ is the most High, God over all, higher than the kings of the earth and highly exalted as Mediator at the right hand of God; and being the mighty God he is mightier than all his enemies, and than the noise they make and the force they use — stronger than the strong man armed, than Satan and all his principalities, than the persecuting princes and potentates of this world, than antichrist, yea than the mighty waves of the sea, which he takes for the same thing under another figure.

The testimonies at the close draw three readings. Gill sets aside the works of nature and providence, and then the Scriptures themselves, as what is chiefly meant, preferring the promises of God — those especially which respect his kingdom and its glory, stability and eternity, being the principal subjects of the psalm — all of them sure and certain, true and faithful, firm, and to be believed. Wesley reads them the same way, as promises which no less than the precepts are God's testimonies, the witnesses or declarations of his will to mankind, and thinks the psalmist speaks of those precious promises concerning the erecting of the Messiah's kingdom. Clarke ties the certainty to the throne: thou wilt as surely fulfil thy word as thou wilt keep possession of thy seat. Ellicott takes the verse in close connection with the one before it, the permanence of the covenant and of the outward signs that attest it being to the Israelite a proof that the divine power is superior to the forces of nature — and he extends the thought, that the moral law is a truer evidence of the existence of God than the uniformity of natural laws.

On the holiness that becomes God's house Clarke writes at most length and widens it as he goes. God's nature is holy, all his works are holy and his word is holy, and therefore his Church should be holy: the building consecrated to his worship alone, the ministers holy, the members holy, the ordinances holy, and its faith, discipline and practice holy — and this at all times, since the phrase means for length of days, during the whole lapse of time, till the sun and moon shall be no more. He passes on the old Psalter's reading that the house of God is man's soul, of which house holiness is the ornament, producing that meek and quiet spirit which is in the sight of God of great price; and he adds that no decoration of person nor simplicity of dress can supply the place of that heavenly clothing. Wesley says the same in a line: it becometh God's people to be holy in all their approach to him.
